newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Feb 5.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Wednesday:

* WMX Technologies said it will sell $1.5 billion in assets and return its focus to waste management services, but investors reacted instead to the company's fourth-quarter loss and its prediction that 1997 earnings would reach only $1.75 a share.
* Apple Computer shifted some of its top management but failed to announce the broad restructuring that analysts were awaiting.

* PepsiCo's earnings fell 85 percent in the fourth quarter on large losses in its international beverage business and slow profits at two of its three fast food chains. The company's shares fell 1-1/4 to 32-7/8.
* Sales of new homes fell one percent and the Index of Leading Economic Indicators rose a tenth of one percent in December.
* The yield on the 30-year Treasury bonds fell to 6.70 percent from 6.73.
* Pilots for AMR's American Airlines set out their contract demands to analysts as the deadline for a strike nears.

* The feud within the family that controls Dow Jones & Co got more complex with a younger member of the Bancroft family saying she is "growing more concerned by the day about the governance and direction of the company" in a letter to other family members.

* Ford Motor's sales rose 2.8 percent in January and Toyota Motor's sales jumped 55.5 percent. Over all, auto sales in the U.S. rose 6.3 percent, but American auto makers lost ground to foreign car companies.

* The Securities and Exchange Commission is asking a Federal judge to reconsider a decision making it tougher for investor lawsuits to proceed under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.
* Sprint posted the strongest annual volume growth among the top three long distance phone companies in seven years and said profits from operations were $0.65 a share.
* True North Communications said it would acquire Wilkins International in Hamburg, Germany, which has a European ad agency network.
* Power plant developer and operator AES Corp said it has a deal to provide electricity to GPU Inc, which owns utilities in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
* Cable and Wireless confirmed it is talking with Germany's Vega AG regarding their differences over the future of their telecommunications joint venture.

* Sarah Ferguson may be scorned in Britain, but infamy sells in America and companies such as H.J. Heinz, which has a contract with the Duchess of York to tout its Weight Watchers business, have a history of hiring rebels for their ads.
* A survey shows New York City is becoming a magnet for venture-capital investments in start-up companies offering new-media and Internet-related services.

* Van Kampen American Capital Growth fund, which rose 62 percent last year, began offering shares to the public on Monday. For investors, the question is not whether shares will be readily available but whether the fund can stay ahead of the pack once it loses its special status.
